Chapter 1: Discovering Injustice—Early Encounters with the System
Sometimes, that first encounter with injustice doesn't crash in with sirens or gavel bangs. Instead, it sneaks up on you—a quiet conversation, a lingering question, or a story you just can't shake.
For one young law student, the world of criminal justice didn't open up inside a grand courtroom. No, it all started in a cramped little office, buried in paperwork, surrounded by the weight of people’s lives. It was just supposed to be a summer internship. Picture the Deep South—air heavy with history, a place where the past is never really gone.
The assignment sounded simple enough: help folks on death row make sense of the legal maze that decided whether they'd live or die. But the truth? Nothing about it was simple. Every case file was more than just paper—it was a life, and every page seemed to whisper a story that nobody had bothered to hear. The people behind those files? Most were poor, some couldn't even read, and almost all had been forgotten by the world outside those prison walls.
One of the very first cases was a man sentenced to die for a crime he swore he hadn’t committed. He was soft-spoken, carried himself with a quiet dignity that just didn’t fit the harshness of his sentence. Meeting him for the first time, the law student felt a mix of fear and responsibility. The prison itself was intimidating. Guards barely looked up, and the rules reminded everyone, every minute, who really had the power. But in that tiny visiting room, something unexpected happened.
The man was genuinely grateful for even the smallest act of kindness—a handshake, a promise to really listen. It hit home just how rare simple compassion was in a place like that.
Pretty quickly, it became obvious: the legal system wasn’t just about laws and evidence. It was about people. People failed by poverty, by racism, by a society that often finds it easier to look away. The student saw how fast someone could get swept up by the system, how one mistake—or even just an accusation—could spiral out of control into a nightmare. The more time spent with these clients, the blurrier the lines got between guilt and innocence. What mattered most wasn’t just whether someone had committed a crime, but whether they’d ever been given a real, fair chance.
Most folks have no idea how much a trial’s outcome can hinge on things that have nothing to do with the facts: the color of a person’s skin, how much money they have, the mood of a judge, or even how sharp their lawyer is. Down South, all those things were magnified by a history of segregation and suspicion. The law student learned quickly—justice wasn’t blind. If anything, it saw exactly what it wanted to see.
By the end of the summer, that experience left a mark that wouldn’t fade. The stories of those men and women on death row weren’t just legal puzzles—they were reminders of how easily mercy gets lost in a system focused on punishment. The student went back to law school changed, still carrying the faces and voices of people the world had left behind.
The future felt uncertain, but one thing was clear: fighting for justice would take more than just legal expertise. It would take empathy, real courage, and a willingness to stand beside those the world had forgotten.
